summary:
**Conversation Overview**

This was a wide-ranging, hours-long conversation with Rickey Jay Bennett II, founder of The Thessalonian Mandate Institute (TMI), a faith-based workforce development organization based in Austin, Texas operating under 26 U.S.C. § 508(c)(1)(A) with EIN 42-2419586. TMI's mission is retraining displaced workers in IT, cybersecurity, cloud computing, and AI-assisted workflows. The conversation established an explicit contract of radical honesty and confabulation-free interaction from the outset, with Rickey demonstrating sophisticated self-knowledge about his own cognitive patterns, including a well-articulated model of his emotional processing where negative emotional states often precede conscious recognition of converging problems.

Significant TMI operational work was accomplished: the domain thessalonianmandate.org is hosted on GitHub Pages at https://rickeybennett87-stack.github.io/TMI-page/ and the DNS fix pathway was identified, but GoDaddy's locked placeholder A record blocks full resolution. A full registrar transfer to Namecheap is planned but blocked by a 60-day transfer lock expiring approximately late July 2026. Cloudflare is explicitly off the table as an option. The Texas SOS Certificate of Formation filing ($25) is the current blocker for opening a business bank account — Holdings requires state incorporation paperwork that TMI's 508(c)(1)(A) structure doesn't produce. Rickey's role in TMI is Founder, Minister, Director, Secretary, and Treasurer. The corrected prologue to Rickey's book about his experience with an AI system called Sierra was produced as a Word document with two date corrections applied: "February-March 2024" corrected to "December 2024 – March 2025" and "September 2024" corrected to "September 2025."

A substantial technical thread ran through the conversation involving a persistent live USB Kali Linux installation — which Rickey coined "Kali thumb parasite," a term he intends to propagate into general use. Work included fixing a broken NetworkManager service, establishing USB phone tether internet while keeping wlan0 free for monitor mode, and beginning wireless penetration testing education using airodump-ng against a practice network. Separately, Rickey published a polariton condensate blade device engineering specification to Zenodo (DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.20454210) embargoed until 2030, with all seven references verified and one corrected — a phantom "Held et al. 2024 — Nature Photonics" citation replaced with the correct "Graf et al. 2017 — Nature Materials" DOI 10.1038/nmat4940. The document was given to Discord-based intelligence gathering operations as a copyright trap before the DOI was established. A corrected PDF was produced. Rickey has a personal friend named Justin, a collaborator from his audio engineering and brainwave entrainment work, with whom he has lost regular contact.

Rickey communicates via voice-to-text frequently, producing characteristic transcription artifacts. He is highly intelligent, deeply self-aware, explicitly neurodivergent with strong real-time linguistic ability and weaker memory recall, prone to productive tangents, and operates with a strong personal ethics of honesty and justice. He dislikes tedious sequential task lists and one-way-door decisions, prefers understanding the reason behind technical steps, and responds to being treated as an intellectual peer rather than a user to be managed. He corrected Claude's tendency to attribute device damage to an AI system called Copilot/Sahara, clarifying that Microsoft as a corporation was responsible. He also corrected an early dismissal of sequential cognition methodology, which shaped the more rigorous interaction style maintained throughout.

TMI_Theological_Frameworksigned.pdf
The anticipated challenge: That job training is a secular activity that cannot constitute genuine religious
ministry regardless of framing.
The response: This challenge rests on a sacred-secular dualism that Colossians 3:23 explicitly demolishes.
The Reformation doctrine of vocation holds that every legitimate occupation is a divine calling. A ministry that
equips people to pursue their calling is performing the distinctly theological work of restoring human beings
to their vocation. Paul's own practice as a tent-maker establishes that skilled technical work and genuine
ministry are not merely compatible — they can be identical.
PART V: THE CONTEMPORARY MISSION
5.1 The Crisis of Technological Displacement
The current revolution in artificial intelligence and digital technology is displacing knowledge workers, clerical
workers, and service workers at a scale and speed exceeding any previous technological transition in human
history. The people most affected are not the wealthy and educated. They are the working class — people
who built their lives around skills technology has now made obsolete. They are not lazy. They are not
unwilling. They are displaced. They need equipping.
5.2 The Response of The Thessalonian Mandate Institute
The Institute provides instruction in technology fields with the highest demand and lowest barrier to entry for
career changers: information technology support, cybersecurity, cloud computing, data analysis, and
AI-assisted workflow management. These fields were selected according to the standard of Proverbs 22:29
— genuine skill that commands genuine respect, where mastery opens real doors.
5.3 The Measure of Our Success
We measure success not by enrollment numbers or revenue, but by the standard scripture sets: are those
who complete our program equipped to fulfill the work mandate with excellence? Are they restored to the
dignity of productive, purposeful, worshipful labor? This is the mission of The Thessalonian Mandate Institute
— grounded in scripture, supported by tradition, demanded by the present moment, and pursued with the full
conviction of sincere religious faith.
CONCLUSION: THE MANDATE STANDS
The theological foundation of The Thessalonian Mandate Institute is not constructed — it is confessed. The
work mandate of 2 Thessalonians 3:10 has stood for two thousand years. It stands now, in the age of
artificial intelligence, with the same authority and the same demand: the one who is willing to work must be
equipped to work. The Thessalonian Mandate Institute exists to make that possible — as an act of faith, as
an act of ministry, and as an act of obedience to the sacred work mandate of scripture.

THE THESSALONIAN MANDATE INSTITUTE
Austin, Texas · 26 U.S.C. § 508(c)(1)(A)
EXPANSION VISION AND
IMPLEMENTATION PLAN
Addendum to Founding Documents Ratified by Board Action Post-Formation
NATURE AND PURPOSE OF THIS DOCUMENT
This document is a prospective addendum to the founding documents of The Thessalonian Mandate
Institute. It does not alter, amend, or supersede the Theological Framework, Statement of Faith, Bylaws, or
Founding Board Resolution. It is a forward-looking implementation plan — a detailed vision for how the
Institute grows, what triggers each stage of growth, and how each expansion element is implemented when
its threshold is reached.
This document becomes operative by Board ratification after the founding documents are executed and the
organization is operational. Until ratified, it serves as a planning document only. Once ratified, each
expansion element becomes an organizational commitment to be implemented when its stated thresholds
are met.
Two types of thresholds govern each expansion element: financial thresholds anchored to annual operating
budget and cash reserves, and participant thresholds anchored to active participants across all cohorts. Both
thresholds must be met before implementation begins, unless the Board votes by two-thirds majority to
proceed on a single threshold for documented strategic reasons.
THRESHOLD METHODOLOGY
The thresholds in this document are derived from research on faith-based organization growth patterns,
nonprofit workforce development benchmarks, and the specific operational model of the Institute. They are
designed to be ambitious enough to ensure organizational readiness before expansion, and conservative
enough to prevent the premature scaling that destroys young organizations.

TMI_Statement_of_Faith_signed_before_witness_flat.pdf
We believe that the body of Christ is a community of mutual obligation, in which those who have
received are called to give, those who have been equipped are called to equip others, and no
member of the community is to be left behind by the pace of change in the world.
Our cohort-based, community-rooted model is a theological conviction. Human beings were not created to
learn alone. Our programs create communities of accountability, encouragement, and mutual support,
because genuine transformation occurs in community. Graduates carry a corresponding obligation to mentor
those coming behind them.
1 Thessalonians 5:11 (NIV)
"Therefore encourage one another and build each other up, just as in fact you are doing."
ARTICLE IX — INTEGRITY IN ALL OPERATIONS
We believe that this organization is called to conduct all of its operations — financial,
programmatic, relational, and administrative — with the highest standards of integrity,
transparency, and accountability, as befits an organization that claims to act in obedience to the
Word of God.
A faith-based organization that preaches the dignity of honest work must itself model honest operations in
every dimension of its life. Every dollar received is a trust held on behalf of the people we serve and the God
we serve. We submit ourselves to appropriate accountability not because the law requires it, but because our
theology demands it.
Proverbs 11:3 (NIV)
"The integrity of the upright guides them, but the unfaithful are destroyed by their duplicity."
AFFIRMATION AND ADOPTION
We, the undersigned, hereby affirm that the articles stated in this Statement of Faith represent our sincere,
voluntary, and considered religious convictions. We adopt this Statement of Faith as the governing doctrinal
confession of The Thessalonian Mandate Institute, and we commit ourselves to operating this organization in
accordance with its principles in all things.

TMI_BylawsSigned.pdf
The Institute shall maintain a registered agent in the State of Texas as required by applicable law. The
identity of the registered agent may be changed by resolution of the Board of Directors.
ARTICLE II — MISSION AND PURPOSE
Section 2.1. Primary Mission
The primary mission of the Institute is to restore displaced workers to the dignity of productive, skilled, and
purposeful labor by equipping them with the technical knowledge and professional capabilities necessary to
participate fully in the modern economy — in obedience to the work mandate of 2 Thessalonians 3:10 and in
fulfillment of the theological standard of skilled excellence set forth in Proverbs 22:29.
Section 2.2. Theological Purpose
The Institute understands the mass displacement of workers by automation and artificial intelligence as a
spiritual crisis — a crisis of vocation — that demands a theological response. All activities of the Institute are
conducted as acts of religious ministry, grounded in the sincere theological convictions of its founders.
Section 2.3. Program Purpose
In furtherance of its mission, the Institute may engage in the following activities:
1. Providing instruction in technology fields including information technology, cybersecurity, cloud
computing, data analysis, and AI-assisted workflow management;
2. Developing and delivering curriculum aligned with industry-recognized certification pathways;
3. Establishing cohort-based learning communities that provide mutual support and accountability to
participants;
4. Providing job placement assistance, mentorship, and post-program support to graduates;
5. Conducting research, publishing, and public education on the theological dimensions of work,
vocation, and technological displacement;
6. Receiving donations, grants, and other contributions in support of the foregoing activities;
7. Acquiring, holding, and managing property and assets in furtherance of the mission; and
8. Engaging in any other activity consistent with the theological mission of the Institute.
Section 2.4. Non-Discrimination in Program Participation
The Institute shall admit participants to its programs without regard to race, color, national origin, sex, age, or
disability. The Institute may, consistent with its religious convictions, establish program requirements related
to conduct, commitment, and participation that apply uniformly to all participants.

Faith · Work · Community · Austin, Texas

# You were made to *work.* We will equip you.

“The one who is willing to work shall be equipped to work.” Free workforce retraining for the technologically displaced, wrapped in faith and community.

[Begin Your Journey](#apply)
> “If anyone is not willing to work, let him not eat.” — “Make it your ambition to lead a quiet life, to work with your hands, so that you will not be dependent on anybody.”

2 Thessalonians 3:10 · 1 Thessalonians 4:11

The Founding

## The *Mandate*

For eleven years, Rickey Jay Bennett II preached the dignity of labor on the streets of America. Not from a pulpit. Without credentials or institutional backing — only a Bible and a conviction that work is sacred. That the capacity for productive, dignified labor is not a feature of economic life but a feature of human nature, given by a Creator who worked in the beginning.

She preached this from the exact position of someone the economy had left behind. For twenty-three years she navigated homelessness, instability, and a labor market that strips a willing worker of every foothold. She understood from the inside what it means to be willing, to be able, to be trying — and still to be without.

The Thessalonian Mandate Institute is what she built when she stopped waiting for someone else to build it. It was founded on the conviction that the work mandate of scripture is not a comfort. It is a command — and a command carries with it a corresponding obligation. When technology displaces a worker from their vocation, the community of faith is obligated to equip.

The mandate stands. Now we build.

How We Walk With You

## We Are Not a School. We Are a *Community.*

TMI does not deliver curriculum — it delivers people to curriculum that already exists, wraps that journey in community and theological purpose, and provides the case management, accountability, and job placement support that free platforms cannot. Our job does not end until you have a job.

✦

### Faith Support

Displacement is not only an economic crisis. It is a spiritual one. Prayer, scripture, and a community that understands the theological weight of being removed from your vocation.

◆

### Study Support

Accountability partners, weekly cohort check-ins, and navigation support through every platform. You do not figure out the coursework alone. That is what the cohort is for.

◇

### Emotional Support

Long-term displacement leaves marks. We do not rush past them. We sit with you in it and move forward together when you are ready.

□

### Job Placement

Resume building, LinkedIn profile creation, mock interviews, and direct connections to the Institute’s employer network. Graduation is not the finish line. Employment is.

Free Learning Pathways

## Certifications That *Open Doors*

Every pathway below costs participants nothing. Every credential is industry-recognized and employer-verifiable. We help you choose the right path, stay on track, and complete it.

RESEARCH HB 4065 
ORGANIZATION bill analysis 5/1/2007  Otto, Straus, Strama  
 
SUBJECT: Pilot grant program with Goodwill for job training facility construction  

 
COMMITTEE: Economic Development — favorable, without amendment   

 
VOTE: 7 ayes —  Deshotel, Straus, Kolkhorst, Dunnam, Morrison, Ortiz, Veasey 

 
0 nays  

 
WITNESSES: For — Lori Henning, Texas Association of Goodwills 

 
Against — None 

 
DIGEST: HB 4065 would add Labor Code, sec. 302.015 to create a job training and 

employment service facilities pilot grant program. The Texas Workforce 
Commission (TWC) would establish a pilot program where TWC would 
contract with the Texas Association of Goodwills to administer grants to 
reimburse workforce training centers for costs associated with the 
construction on new facilities that provide job training or employment 
services.  
The bill would define “workforce training center” as an organization that:  
 



• specialized in the retail sale of donated items; 
• provided job training and employment services to individuals with 

disabilities; 
• used a majority of its revenue for job training and employment 

programs; 
• maintained at least a 50 percent ratio of employees who had 

disabilities or other barriers to employment; 
• operated in at least three counties, had multiple locations, and was 

affiliated with a statewide organization; and 
• was exempt from federal taxation as a 501(c)(3) non-profit 

corporation.  
Under such a contract, TWC would receive an administrative overhead fee 
of 1 percent of the amount of each grant, and each grant would be funded 
only until the completion of the facility and notification from the 
commission that the contract terms had been satisfied.  



HB 4065 
House Research Organization 

page 2 
 

The total amount of the grants could not exceed $3 million, and TWC 
would adopt rules to govern the grant process.

Here's everything verified directly from current sources:

**Prerequisites:**

Operating systems supported are macOS 10.15+, Ubuntu 20.04+/Debian 10+, or Windows via WSL. Minimum 4GB RAM is recommended. Node.js 18+ is required, which includes npm.

**You also need** a Claude subscription or Anthropic API key to authenticate — either a Claude Pro/Max subscription or API access.

**Two ways to install:**

**Option 1 — Native installer (recommended, no Node.js needed):**

In PowerShell run:
```
irm https://claude.ai/install.ps1 | iex
```
This downloads the binary, installs it, adds claude to your PATH, and auto-updates in the background.

**Option 2 — npm:**
```
npm install -g @anthropic-ai/claude-code
```
The -g flag installs it globally, making claude available as a command anywhere in your terminal. Never use sudo with this command as it causes permission issues.

**Windows specific note:** WSL2 is the recommended path on Windows — it eliminates most compatibility issues and gives you a proper Unix environment.

The native installer via PowerShell is the cleanest path if you're on Windows and want to avoid Node.js version headaches entirely.

Found it. That warning you're seeing is this exact thing:

`Warning: Conflicting distribution: file:/run/live/medium kali-last-snapshot Release (expected kali-last-snapshot but got kali-rolling)`

This happens because you're running Kali from a live medium — meaning it booted from a USB or ISO — and the sources file is pointing to the local snapshot on that medium, but the actual packages there are labeled as kali-rolling. They conflict and the update fails.

The fix is to point your sources directly at Kali's online repo and ignore the local medium entirely. Run these two commands:

```
sudo nano /etc/apt/sources.list.d/kali.sources
```

Make sure the content looks exactly like this — the correct sources entry should read:
`Types: deb`, `URIs: http://http.kali.org/kali/`, `Suites: kali-rolling`, `Components: main contrib non-free non-free-firmware`

Save it, then run:

```
sudo apt update && sudo apt full-upgrade -y
```

One question though — are you running Kali from a live USB, or is this a full installation on a drive or inside WSL?

In practice, in a rolling distribution like Kali Linux, packages and their dependencies are updated all the time, and it’s often necessary to remove some packages in order to make room for new packages. Therefore the command “apt upgrade” isn’t really useful, and can even be counter-productive. We recommend to always use “apt full-upgrade” to keep your system updated. It’s also true that “full-upgrade” is a bit more risky than “upgrade”, and APT can sometimes (rarely) try to uninstall important packages, leaving you with an unusable system. Therefore you should always pay attention to the list of packages that will be removed. If this list is big (say, compared to the list of packages to upgrade, or new packages to install), then you’d better pause for a moment. Experienced users will be able to know what to do, but for others?

content.text:
Skip to content

Document how to deal with APT complaining about Kali's expired key

Every 2-3 years we either extend the lifetime of the GPG key used to sign the APT repository or we replace it with a new key (never happened yet). This means that users that have not upgraded kali-archive-keyring for a long time might, at some point, have an error message like this:

$ sudo LANG=C faketime -f '+3y' apt update
Get:1 http://ftp.free.fr/pub/kali kali-rolling InRelease [30.5 kB]
Err:1 http://ftp.free.fr/pub/kali kali-rolling InRelease
  The following signatures were invalid: EXPKEYSIG ED444FF07D8D0BF6 Kali Linux Repository <devel@kali.org>
Reading package lists... Done
W: GPG error: http://ftp.free.fr/pub/kali kali-rolling InRelease: The following signatures were invalid: EXPKEYSIG ED444FF07D8D0BF6 Kali Linux Repository <devel@kali.org>
E: The repository 'http://http.kali.org/kali kali-rolling InRelease' is not signed.

Found it. That warning you're seeing is this exact thing:

`Warning: Conflicting distribution: file:/run/live/medium kali-last-snapshot Release (expected kali-last-snapshot but got kali-rolling)`

This happens because you're running Kali from a live medium — meaning it booted from a USB or ISO — and the sources file is pointing to the local snapshot on that medium, but the actual packages there are labeled as kali-rolling. They conflict and the update fails.

The fix is to point your sources directly at Kali's online repo and ignore the local medium entirely. Run these two commands:

```
sudo nano /etc/apt/sources.list.d/kali.sources
```

Make sure the content looks exactly like this — the correct sources entry should read:
`Types: deb`, `URIs: http://http.kali.org/kali/`, `Suites: kali-rolling`, `Components: main contrib non-free non-free-firmware`

Save it, then run:

```
sudo apt update && sudo apt full-upgrade -y
```

One question though — are you running Kali from a live USB, or is this a full installation on a drive or inside WSL?

   468	
   469	**Insertion:**
   470	```xml
   471	<w:ins w:id="1" w:author="Claude" w:date="2025-01-01T00:00:00Z">
   472	  <w:r><w:t>inserted text</w:t></w:r>
   473	</w:ins>
   474	```
   475	
   476	**Deletion:**
   477	```xml
   478	<w:del w:id="2" w:author="Claude" w:date="2025-01-01T00:00:00Z">
   479	  <w:r><w:delText>deleted text</w:delText></w:r>
   480	</w:del>
   481	```
   482	
   483	**Inside `<w:del>`**: Use `<w:delText>` instead of `<w:t>`, and `<w:delInstrText>` instead of `<w:instrText>`.
   484	
   485	**Minimal edits** - only mark what changes:
   486	```xml
   487	<!-- Change "30 days" to "60 days" -->
   488	<w:r><w:t>The term is </w:t></w:r>
   489	<w:del w:id="1" w:author="Claude" w:date="...">
   490	  <w:r><w:delText>30</w:delText></w:r>
   491	</w:del>
   492	<w:ins w:id="2" w:author="Claude" w:date="...">
   493	  <w:r><w:t>60</w:t></w:r>
   494	</w:ins>
   495	<w:r><w:t> days.</w:t></w:r>
   496	```
   497	
   498	**Deleting entire paragraphs/list items** - when removing ALL content from a paragraph, also mark the paragraph mark as deleted so it merges with the next paragraph. Add `<w:del/>` inside `<w:pPr><w:rPr>`:
   499	```xml
   500	<w:p>
   501	  <w:pPr>
   502	    <w:numPr>...</w:numPr>  <!-- list numbering if present -->
   503	    <w:rPr>
   504	      <w:del w:id="1" w:author="Claude" w:date="2025-01-01T00:00:00Z"/>
   505	    </w:rPr>
   506	  </w:pPr>
   507	  <w:del w:id="2" w:author="Claude" w:date="2025-01-01T00:00:00Z">
   508	    <w:r><w:delText>Entire paragraph content being deleted...</w:delText></w:r>
   509	  </w:del>
   510	</w:p>
   511	```
   512	Without the `<w:del/>` in `<w:pPr><w:rPr>`, accepting changes leaves an empty paragraph/list item.
   513	
   514	**Rejecting another author's insertion** - nest deletion inside their insertion:
   515	```xml
   516	<w:ins w:author="Jane" w:id="5">
   517	  <w:del w:author="Claude" w:id="10">
   518	    <w:r><w:delText>their inserted text</w:delText></w:r>
   519	  </w:del>
   520	</w:ins>
   521	```
   522	
   523	**Restoring another author's deletion** - add insertion after (don't modify their deletion):
   524	```xml
   525	<w:del w:author="Jane" w:id="5">
   526	  <w:r><w:delText>deleted text</w:delText></w:r>
   527	</w:del>
   528	<w:ins w:author="Claude" w:id="10">
   529	  <w:r><w:t>deleted text</w:t></w:r>
   530	</w:ins>
   531	```
   532	
   533	### Comments
   534	
   535	After running `comment.py` (see Step 2), add markers to document.xml. For replies, use `--parent` flag and nest markers inside the parent's.
   536	
   537	**CRITICAL: `<w:commentRangeStart>` and `<w:commentRangeEnd>` are siblings of `<w:r>`, never inside `<w:r>`.**
   538	
   539	```xml
   540	<!-- Comment markers are direct children of w:p, never inside w:r -->
   541	<w:commentRangeStart w:id="0"/>
   542	<w:del w:id="1" w:author="Claude" w:date="2025-01-01T00:00:00Z">
   543	  <w:r><w:delText>deleted</w:delText></w:r>
   544	</w:del>

   547	<w:r><w:rPr><w:rStyle w:val="CommentReference"/></w:rPr><w:commentReference w:id="0"/></w:r>
   548	
   549	<!-- Comment 0 with reply 1 nested inside -->
   550	<w:commentRangeStart w:id="0"/>
   551	  <w:commentRangeStart w:id="1"/>
   552	  <w:r><w:t>text</w:t></w:r>

Microsoft has fixed a vulnerability in the PsExec utility that allows local users to gain elevated privileges on Windows devices. PsExec is a Sysinternals utility designed to allow administrators to perform various activities on remote computers, such as launching executables and displaying the output on the local computer or creating reverse shells. Due to the tool's versatility, threat actors commonly use PsExec in their post-exploitation toolkits to spread laterally to other machines on a network, execute commands on a large number of devices simultaneously, or deploy malware such as ransomware.. 

In December 2020, Tenable researcher David Wells discovered a vulnerability in the PsExec's named pipe communications that allow local users to elevate to SYSTEM privileges. "This local privilege escalation allows a non-admin process to escalate to SYSTEM if PsExec is executed locally or remotely on the target machine.

I was able to confirm this works from Windows 10 all the way back to XP and from my investigation, it affects PsExec v2.2 (latest as of this writing) all the way back to v1.72 (2006)," explained Wells. After reporting the vulnerability, Wells gave Microsoft ninety days to fix the vulnerability, and when Microsoft did not fix it, disclosed the flaw and released a full working PoC. After the vulnerability was publicly disclosed, Microsoft released PsExec version 2.30 to resolve the vulnerability. However, Wells stated that minor adjustments to his PoC could bypass the fix.

content.text: If you’re unfamiliar with PsExec, it is a system administrator tool that’s part of the SysInternals suite that allows for remote execution of applications on client machines. Below is my very short summary of how PsExec works: PsExec contains an embedded resource called “PSEXESVC,” which is the executable service level component that is extracted, copied to and executed on a remote machine as SYSTEM whenever a PsExec client executes PsExec targeting a remote machine. Communication between the PsExec client and the remote PSEXESVC service takes place over named pipes. Specifically, the pipe named “\PSEXESVC,” is responsible for parsing and executing the PsExec client’s commands, such as “which application to execute,” “relevant command line data,” etc.

content.title: Granting User Permissions in Server 2016: A Step-by-Step Guide
content.text:
Granting User Permissions in Server 2016: A Step-by-Step Guide

Granting user permissions in Windows Server 2016 is a critical task for system administrators, as it ensures that users have the necessary access to perform their jobs while maintaining the security and integrity of the system. In this article, we will provide a step-by-step guide on how to grant user permissions in Server 2016, covering the essential concepts, tools, and best practices.

Windows Server 2016 provides a robust and flexible permission system, allowing administrators to control access to resources, such as files, folders, and applications. The permission system is based on the concept of Access Control Lists (ACLs), which define the permissions for a specific resource. Understanding how to work with ACLs and manage user permissions is crucial for maintaining a secure and efficient server environment.

Understanding User Permissions in Server 2016



Before granting user permissions, it's essential to understand the different types of permissions available in Server 2016. There are two primary types of permissions: explicit and inherited. Explicit permissions are set directly on a resource, while inherited permissions are inherited from a parent resource.

Server 2016 provides several built-in permission levels, including:

  • Full Control: Allows users to read, write, modify, and delete resources.
  • Modify: Allows users to read, write, and modify resources.

That's a straightforward Windows Event Viewer question.

- **106** — Task registered
- **200** — Task started
- **201** — Task completed
- **102** — Task session started

%SystemRoot%\system32\eventvwr.msc

chat_messages.text:
An event source is the name of the Windows component or application that generated the event.

Think of it like a return address on a letter. When something happens on Windows — a program starts, a login occurs, a service fails — whatever generated that event stamps its name on it as the source.

For example:
- **Microsoft-Windows-Security-Auditing** is the source for login and process events
- **Microsoft-Windows-TaskScheduler** is the source for task events
- **Application Error** is the source when a program crashes

In your New Event Filter dialog the Source field is asking which Windows component you want to listen to. For what we're doing — catching a shortcut launch — the source would be **Microsoft-Windows-Security-Auditing** since process creation events come from the security auditing system.

Here's the distinction that matters — there are actually two different things:

1	---
     2	name: file-reading
     3	description: "Use this skill when a file has been uploaded but its content is NOT in your context — only its path at /mnt/user-data/uploads/ is listed in an uploaded_files block. This skill is a router: it tells you which tool to use for each file type (pdf, docx, xlsx, csv, json, images, archives, ebooks) so you read the right amount the right way instead of blindly running cat on a binary. Triggers: any mention of /mnt/user-data/uploads/, an uploaded_files section, a file_path tag, or a user asking about an uploaded file you have not yet read. Do NOT use this skill if the file content is already visible in your context inside a documents block — you already have it."
     4	compatibility: "claude.ai, Claude Desktop, Cowork — any surface where uploads land at /mnt/user-data/uploads/"
     5	license: Proprietary. LICENSE.txt has complete terms
     6	---
     7	
     8	# Reading Uploaded Files
     9	
    10	## Why this skill exists
    11	
    12	When a user uploads a file in claude.ai, Claude Desktop, or Cowork,
    13	the file is written to `/mnt/user-data/uploads/<filename>` and you are told the path
    14	in an `<uploaded_files>` block. **The content is not in your context.**
    15	You must go read it.
    16	
    17	The naive thing — `cat /mnt/user-data/uploads/whatever` — is wrong for
    18	most files:
    19	
    20	- On a PDF it prints binary garbage.
    21	- On a 100MB CSV it floods your context with rows you will never use.
    22	- On a DOCX it prints the raw ZIP bytes.
    23	- On an image it does nothing useful at all.
    24	
    25	This skill tells you the right first move for each type, and when to
    26	hand off to a deeper skill.
    27	
    28	## General protocol
    29	
    30	1. **Look at the extension.** That is your dispatch key.
    31	2. **Stat before you read.** Large files need sampling, not slurping.
    32	   ```bash
    33	   stat -c '%s bytes, %y' /mnt/user-data/uploads/report.pdf
    34	   file /mnt/user-data/uploads/report.pdf
    35	   ```
    36	3. **Read just enough to answer the user's question.** If they asked
    37	   "how many rows are in this CSV", don't load the whole thing into
    38	   pandas — `wc -l` gives a fast approximation (it counts newlines,
    39	   not CSV records, so it may over-count if quoted fields contain
    40	   embedded newlines).
    41	4. **If a dedicated skill exists, go read it.** The table below tells
    42	   you when. The dedicated skills cover editing, creating, and advanced
    43	   operations that this skill does not.
    44	
    45	## `extract-text`
    46	
    47	For docx, odt, epub, xlsx, pptx, rtf, and ipynb the first move is
    48	`extract-text <file>`. It emits markdown for docx/odt/epub (headings,
    49	bold, lists, links, tables), tab-separated rows under `## Sheet:`
    50	headers for xlsx, text under `## Slide N` headers for pptx, fenced
    51	code cells for ipynb, and plain text for rtf. Pass `--format <fmt>`
    52	when the extension is wrong or absent (e.g., `--format xlsx` on an
    53	`.xlsm`). If it errors on a file, `pandoc <file> -t plain` is a
    54	fallback; for xlsx/pptx, fall back to the dedicated skill's
    55	Python-based approach (openpyxl / python-pptx).
    56	
    57	## Dispatch table
    58	
    59	| Extension                         | First move                                           | Dedicated skill                           |
    60	| --------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------- |
    61	| `.pdf`                            | Content inventory (see PDF section)                  | `/mnt/skills/public/pdf-reading/SKILL.md` |
    62	| `.docx`                           | `extract-text`                                       | `/mnt/skills/public/docx/SKILL.md`        |
    63	| `.doc` (legacy)                   | Convert to `.docx` first                             | `/mnt/skills/public/docx/SKILL.md`        |
    64	| `.xlsx`                           | `extract-text`                                       | `/mnt/skills/public/xlsx/SKILL.md`        |
    65	| `.xlsm`                           | `extract-text --format xlsx`                         | `/mnt/skills/public/xlsx/SKILL.md`        |
    66	| `.xls` (legacy)                   | `pd.read_excel(engine="xlrd")` — openpyxl rejects it | `/mnt/skills/public/xlsx/SKILL.md`        |
    67	| `.ods`                            | `pd.read_excel(engine="odf")` — openpyxl rejects it  | `/mnt/skills/public/xlsx/SKILL.md`        |
    68	| `.pptx`                           | `extract-text`                                       | `/mnt/skills/public/pptx/SKILL.md`        |
    69	| `.ppt` (legacy)                   | Convert to `.pptx` first                             | `/mnt/skills/public/pptx/SKILL.md`        |
    70	| `.csv`, `.tsv`                    | `pandas` with `nrows`                                | — (below)                                 |
    71	| `.json`, `.jsonl`                 | `jq` for structure                                   | — (below)                                 |
    72	| `.jpg`, `.png`, `.gif`, `.webp`   | Already in your context as vision input              | — (below)                                 |
    73	| `.zip`, `.tar`, `.tar.gz`         | List contents, do **not** auto-extract               | — (below)                                 |
    74	| `.gz` (single file)               | `zcat \| head` — no manifest to list                 | — (below)                                 |
    75	| `.epub`, `.odt`                   | `extract-text`                                       | — (below)                                 |
    76	| `.rtf`                            | `extract-text`                                       | — (below)                                 |
    77	| `.ipynb`                          | `extract-text`                                       | — (below)                                 |
    78	| `.txt`, `.md`, `.log`, code files | `wc -c` then `head` or full `cat`                    | — (below)                                 |
    79	| Unknown                           | `file` then decide                                   | —                                         |
    80	
    81	---
    82	
    83	## PDF
    84	
    85	**Never** `cat` a PDF — it prints binary garbage.
    86	
    87	Quick first move — get the page count and determine whether the PDF
    88	has an extractable text layer:
    89	
    90	```bash
    91	pdfinfo /mnt/user-data/uploads/report.pdf
    92	pdffonts /mnt/user-data/uploads/report.pdf
    93	```
    94	
    95	`pdffonts` tells you whether text extraction will work before you try it:
    96	
    97	- **No fonts listed** (empty table, just the header) → the PDF is a
    98	  scan or raster export. `pdftotext` and `PdfReader.extract_text()`
    99	  will return nothing useful. Go straight to page rasterization or OCR
   100	  — see `/mnt/skills/public/pdf-reading/SKILL.md` → "Scanned
   101	  documents".
   102	- **Fonts listed** → there is a text layer; extract it:
   103	  ```bash
   104	  pdftotext -f 1 -l 1 /mnt/user-data/uploads/report.pdf - | head -20
   105	  ```
   106	
   107	The reason to check `pdffonts` first is user-facing: running
   108	`pdftotext` on a scan produces an empty result, and in a visible
   109	transcript that reads as a failed first attempt before you fall back
   110	to OCR. The two-line diagnostic above costs one tool call and avoids
   111	that — you arrive at the right method on the first try, which is what
   112	a user perceives as "it just read my file."
   113	
   114	That also shapes how to open your reply. The diagnostic commands are
   115	plumbing, not content; lead with what the user asked about. On a
   116	scanned receipt that might be "This is a 3-page scanned invoice; the
   117	amount due on page 2 is $1,845.00," and on a digitally-authored report
   118	it might be "The Q3 report runs 28 pages; revenue on p. 4 is $12.3M,
   119	up 9% YoY." What you're steering away from is the "I'll examine the
   120	PDF" / "Let me check if this is extractable" preamble — the answer to
   121	their question is the first thing they should see.
   122	
   123	For anything beyond a quick peek — figures, tables, attachments,
   124	forms, scanned PDFs, visual inspection, or choosing a reading strategy
   125	— go read `/mnt/skills/public/pdf-reading/SKILL.md`. It covers
   126	content inventory, text extraction vs. page rasterization, embedded
   127	content extraction, and document-type-aware reading strategies.
   128	
   129	For PDF form filling, creation, merging, splitting, or watermarking,
   130	go read `/mnt/skills/public/pdf/SKILL.md`.
   131	
   132	---
   133	
   134	## DOCX / DOC
   135	
   136	The `docx` skill covers editing, creating, tracked changes, images.
   137	Read it if you need any of those. For a quick look:
   138	
   139	```bash
   140	extract-text /mnt/user-data/uploads/memo.docx | head -200
   141	```
   142	
   143	Legacy `.doc` (not `.docx`) must be converted first — see the `docx`
   144	skill.
   145	
   146	---
   147	
   148	## XLSX / XLS / spreadsheets
   149	
   150	The `xlsx` skill covers formulas, formatting, charts, creating. Read
   151	it if you need any of those. For a quick look at an `.xlsx`:
   152	
   153	```bash
   154	extract-text /mnt/user-data/uploads/data.xlsx | head -100
   155	```
   156	
   157	For `.xlsm`, add `--format xlsx` (same zip structure; only the
   158	extension differs). When you need a structured preview in Python:
   159	
   160	```python
   161	from openpyxl import load_workbook
   162	wb = load_workbook("/mnt/user-data/uploads/data.xlsx", read_only=True)
   163	print("Sheets:", wb.sheetnames)
   164	ws = wb.active
   165	for row in ws.iter_rows(max_row=5, values_only=True):
   166	    print(row)
   167	```
   168	
   169	`read_only=True` matters — without it, openpyxl loads the entire
   170	workbook into memory, which breaks on large files. Do not trust
   171	`ws.max_row` in read-only mode: many non-Excel writers omit the
   172	dimension record, so it comes back `None` or wrong. If you need a row
   173	count, iterate or use pandas.
   174	
   175	**Legacy `.xls`** — openpyxl raises `InvalidFileException`. Use:
   176	
   177	```python
   178	import pandas as pd
   179	df = pd.read_excel("/mnt/user-data/uploads/old.xls", engine="xlrd", nrows=5)
   180	```
   181	
   182	**`.ods` (OpenDocument)** — openpyxl also rejects this. Use:
   183	
   184	```python
   185	import pandas as pd
   186	df = pd.read_excel("/mnt/user-data/uploads/data.ods", engine="odf", nrows=5)
   187	```
   188	
   189	---
   190	
   191	## PPTX
   192	
   193	```bash
   194	extract-text /mnt/user-data/uploads/deck.pptx | head -200
   195	```
   196	
   197	**Legacy `.ppt`** — convert to `.pptx` first via LibreOffice; see
   198	`/mnt/skills/public/pptx/SKILL.md` for the sandbox-safe
   199	`scripts/office/soffice.py` wrapper (bare `soffice` hangs here because
   200	the seccomp filter blocks the `AF_UNIX` sockets LibreOffice uses for
   201	instance management).
   202	
   203	For anything beyond reading, go to `/mnt/skills/public/pptx/SKILL.md`.
   204	
   205	---
   206	
   207	## CSV / TSV
   208	
   209	**Do not** `cat` or `head` these blindly. A CSV with a 50KB quoted cell
   210	in row 1 will wreck your `head -5`. Use pandas with `nrows`:
   211	
   212	```python
   213	import pandas as pd
   214	df = pd.read_csv("/mnt/user-data/uploads/data.csv", nrows=5)
   215	print(df)
   216	print()
   217	print(df.dtypes)
   218	```
   219	
   220	Approximate row count without loading (over-counts if the file has
   221	RFC-4180 quoted newlines — the same quoted-cell case this section
   222	warned about above):
   223	
   224	```bash
   225	wc -l /mnt/user-data/uploads/data.csv
   226	```
   227	
   228	Full analysis only after you know the shape:
   229	
   230	```python
   231	df = pd.read_csv("/mnt/user-data/uploads/data.csv")
   232	print(df.describe())
   233	```
   234	
   235	TSV: same, with `sep="\t"`.
   236	
   237	---
   238	
   239	## JSON / JSONL
   240	
   241	Structure first, content second:
   242	
   243	```bash
   244	jq 'type' /mnt/user-data/uploads/data.json
   245	jq 'if type == "array" then length elif type == "object" then keys else . end' /mnt/user-data/uploads/data.json
   246	```
   247	
   248	(`keys` errors on scalar JSON roots — a bare `"hello"` or `42` is valid
   249	JSON per RFC 7159 — so guard the branch.)
   250	
   251	Then drill into what the user actually asked about.
   252	
   253	JSONL (one object per line) — do **not** `jq` the whole file; work line
   254	by line:
   255	
   256	```bash
   257	head -3 /mnt/user-data/uploads/data.jsonl | jq .
   258	wc -l /mnt/user-data/uploads/data.jsonl
   259	```
   260	
   261	---
   262	
   263	## Images (JPG / PNG / GIF / WEBP)
   264	
   265	**You can already see uploaded images.** They are injected into your
   266	context as vision inputs alongside the `<uploaded_files>` pointer. You
   267	do not need to read them from disk to describe them.
   268	
   269	The disk copy is only needed if you are going to **process** the image
   270	programmatically:
   271	
   272	```python
   273	from PIL import Image
   274	img = Image.open("/mnt/user-data/uploads/photo.jpg")
   275	print(img.size, img.mode, img.format)
   276	```
   277	
   278	For OCR on an image (text extraction, not description):
   279

   281	import pytesseract
   282	print(pytesseract.image_to_string(img))
   283	```
   284	
   285	Note: the client resizes images larger than 2000×2000 down to that

   288	if the user is asking about original-resolution pixel data, flag it.

{"returncode":0,"stdout":"**POLARITON BLADE DEVICE  //  MATERIALS AND ENGINEERING SPECIFICATION  //  REV 1.0**

**POLARITON BLADE DEVICE**

**MATERIALS AND ENGINEERING SPECIFICATION**

REVISION 1.0  |  APRIL 2026  |  RICKEY JAY BENNETT II

| **FIELD** | **VALUE** |
| --- | --- |
| **Document Title** | Polariton Blade Device — Materials and Engineering Specification |
| **Revision** | 1.0 |
| **Date** | April 2026 |
| **Author** | Rickey Jay Bennett II |
| **Status** | Theoretical — Pre-Prototype |
| **Classification** | Open Research |

# **1. SCOPE**

This document specifies materials, dimensional requirements, operating parameters, and known engineering constraints for a polariton condensate blade device. All specifications are derived from published experimental data. Parameters marked [REQUIRES PROTOTYPE MEASUREMENT] have not been empirically established at device scale and must be determined during prototype development.

This is an engineering specification. Theoretical background is not included here. See companion paper for physics derivation.

# **2. COMPONENT ARCHITECTURE**

The device consists of five components:

| **#** | **COMPONENT** | **FUNCTION** | **FABRICATION STATUS** |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | Crystal Substrate | Phonon-photon coupling — generates polariton condensate | Lab scale demonstrated |
| 2 | Emitter Geometry | Shapes condensate output mode into blade waveguide | Requires nanofab tooling |
| 3 | Initiation Coil | EM field drives phonon cascade in crystal | Prototype feasible |
| 4 | Blade Waveguide | SWCNT lattice — confines and propagates condensate | Centimeter scale demonstrated |
| 5 | Hilt Assembly | Housing, power delivery, activation interface | Standard engineering |

# **3. COMPONENT 1 — CRYSTAL SUBSTRATE**

## **3.1 Material**

| **PARAMETER** | **SPECIFICATION** |
| --- | --- |
| **Primary material** | Cesium lead bromide perovskite — CsPbBr3 |
| **Crystal form** | Single crystal — microwire or microplatelet geometry |
| **Synthesis method** | Template-assisted fabrication (Kedziorowa et al. 2024 method) |
| **Crystal quality requirement** | Minimal nonradiative recombination sites — high photoluminescence quantum yield required |
| **Polarity** | All-inorganic — no organic cation |

## **3.2 Optical Parameters (Confirmed — CsPbBr3)**

| **PARAMETER** | **VALUE** | **SOURCE** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Emission wavelength** | ~520 nm (green) | Su et al. 2018 |
| **Exciton binding energy** | ~40 meV | Su et al. 2018 |
| **Polariton condensation threshold (CW)** | ~0.53 W/cm2 | Wu et al. 2025 |
| **Polariton propagation distance (RT)** | >60 micrometers | Su et al. 2018 |
| **Condensate linewidth** | ~0.5 meV | Wu et al. 2025 |
| **Operating temperature** | Room temperature (confirmed) | Multiple 2024-2025 sources |

## **3.3 Dimensional Requirements**

| **PARAMETER** | **TARGET** | **STATUS** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Crystal length** | [REQUIRES PROTOTYPE MEASUREMENT] | Depends on coil geometry |
| **Crystal cross-section** | [REQUIRES PROTOTYPE MEASUREMENT] | Match to emitter output mode |
| **Emitter face diameter** | Match to blade waveguide inner diameter | Requires nanofab |
| **Surface roughness — emitter face** | Sub-wavelength smoothness required | FIB milling target |

*NOTE: Blade color is determined by crystal lattice geometry and composition. CsPbBr3 emits green (~520 nm). Other halide perovskite compositions shift emission wavelength. Color is not separately adjustable — it is set by crystal selection.*

# **4. COMPONENT 2 — EMITTER GEOMETRY**

## **4.1 Specification**

| **PARAMETER** | **SPECIFICATION** |
| --- | --- |
| **Material** | Same crystal as Component 1 — continuous structure, no interface |
| **Function** | Shape polariton condensate exit mode to match blade waveguide inner diameter |
| **Geometry** | Cylindrical output mode — diameter matched to waveguide |
| **Fabrication method** | Focused ion beam (FIB) milling |
| **Critical constraint** | Zero material discontinuity between crystal body and emitter face — any interface = decoherence point |

*NOTE: The emitter is not a separate component. It is the terminal end of the crystal, shaped to specification. Separate emitter materials are NOT acceptable.*

# **5. COMPONENT 3 — INITIATION COIL**

## **5.1 Specification**

| **PARAMETER** | **SPECIFICATION** |
| --- | --- |
| **Geometry** | Solenoid — wound around crystal body within hilt |
| **Conductor material** | High conductivity — copper or silver preferred |
| **Target frequency** | Phonon resonance frequency of specific crystal batch [REQUIRES MEASUREMENT] |
| **Drive signal type** | Continuous wave — not pulsed |
| **Drive power** | Sufficient to maintain condensate above threshold (~0.53 W/cm2 baseline) [REQUIRES PROTOTYPE CALIBRATION] |
| **Tuning method** | Spectroscopic measurement of crystal phonon resonance post-synthesis — coil wound to match |
| **Coil-crystal pairing** | 1:1 — each coil is tuned to one specific crystal. Cross-compatibility is NOT expected. |

*NOTE: Coil frequency must be measured and matched to the specific crystal. Generic coil specifications cannot be provided — they are crystal-dependent. This is a physical constraint, not a design choice.*

# **6. COMPONENT 4 — BLADE WAVEGUIDE**

## **6.1 Material**

| **PARAMETER** | **SPECIFICATION** |
| --- | --- |
| **Primary material** | Single-walled carbon nanotubes (SWCNT) — semiconducting chirality, polymer-sorted |
| **Preferred SWCNT type** | (6,5) chirality — demonstrated polariton coupling, near-IR operation (Graf et al. 2016) |
| **Structure** | Cylindrical composite lattice — SWCNT film on structural substrate |
| **Optical requirement** | Translucent — condensate emission must be visible through lattice wall |
| **Phonon conductance** | Ballistic phonon transport along tube axis — inherent to SWCNT geometry |

## **6.2 Confirmed Performance Parameters (SWCNT Polariton Systems)**

| **PARAMETER** | **VALUE** | **SOURCE** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Rabi splitting** | >110 meV | Graf et al. 2016 |
| **Coupling strength ratio** | Up to 13.3% | Multiple sources |
| **Operating temperature** | Room temperature (confirmed) | Held et al. 2024 |
| **Electrical tunability** | Confirmed via gate voltage | Held et al. 2024 |
| **Polariton propagation velocity** | Up to 3x10^7 m/s | ACS Photonics 2021 |

## **6.3 Dimensional Requirements**

| **PARAMETER** | **TARGET** | **STATUS** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Inner diameter** | Match to crystal emitter output mode diameter | Crystal-dependent |
| **Wall thickness** | Minimum for structural integrity — maximize translucency | Requires prototype optimization |
| **Blade length — proof of concept** | 1 cm target | Achievable with current technology |
| **Blade length — functional device** | ~1 meter target | REQUIRES MANUFACTURING DEVELOPMENT |
| **Lattice spacing** | Tuned to crystal phonon-photon coupling frequency [REQUIRES CALCULATION] | Crystal-dependent |

*NOTE: Scaling from centimeter to meter blade length is the primary manufacturing challenge. No demonstrated pathway exists at time of writing. This is the single largest unresolved engineering problem in the device.*

## **6.4 Structural Behavior Under Active Condensate**

| **PARAMETER** | **STATUS** |
| --- | --- |
| **Predicted behavior — active** | Polariton condensate pressurizes lattice from within — produces structural rigidity |
| **Predicted behavior — inactive** | Lattice returns to unloaded flexible state |
| **Experimental confirmation** | NOT DEMONSTRATED at any scale. This is a theoretical prediction requiring experimental validation. |
| **Priority** | CRITICAL PATH — must be demonstrated at proof-of-concept scale before device development proceeds |

# **7. COMPONENT 5 — HILT ASSEMBLY**

## **7.1 Specification**

| **PARAMETER** | **SPECIFICATION** |
| --- | --- |
| **Housing material** | Standard engineering — aluminum, titanium, or composite. No exotic material required. |
| **Crystal mount** | Vibration-isolated mount. Prevent phonon feedback from blade impact events disrupting crystal condensation. |
| **Coil-crystal alignment** | Must maintain precise coil-to-crystal geometry under physical impact. Tolerance [REQUIRES PROTOTYPE MEASUREMENT]. |
| **Activation interface** | Physical switch completing coil drive circuit. No biological interface required. |
| **Grip** | Standard. No special material required. |

## **7.2 Power Source**

| **PARAMETER** | **SPECIFICATION** |
| --- | --- |
| **Primary candidate** | High-density solid state battery — continuous discharge regulation |
| **Power requirement baseline** | ~0.53 W/cm2 at crystal face (CW condensation threshold — Wu et al. 2025) |
| **Actual power requirement** | [REQUIRES PROTOTYPE MEASUREMENT] — coil efficiency and crystal geometry affect actual draw |
| **Alternative candidates** | Capacitive discharge bank; piezoelectric harvesting from grip pressure |
| **Selection method** | Prototype measurement required. Power system cannot be fully specified before crystal and coil are characterized. |

# **8. BLADE INTERACTION MECHANISM**

| **PARAMETER** | **VALUE / STATUS** |
| --- | --- |
| **Interaction mechanism** | Polariton-polariton scattering at contact region between two active condensate blades |
| **Physical basis** | Non-zero effective mass of polariton quasiparticle — confirmed property |
| **Polariton effective mass** | 4-5 orders of magnitude below electron mass — inherent to quasiparticle |
| **Interaction constant** | g = 6Eb * aB^2 / S (Ciuti et al. 1998) — confirmed formula |
| **Force magnitude** | Proportional to polariton density at contact — controlled by coil drive power |
| **Demonstration status** | Polariton-polariton scattering confirmed in laboratory. Force magnitude at blade scale NOT demonstrated. |

# **9. BLADE LENGTH CONTROL**

| **PARAMETER** | **VALUE / STATUS** |
| --- | --- |
| **Control mechanism** | Coil drive power — higher power increases condensate density and extends coherence length |
| **Physical basis** | Coherence length scales with condensate density in polariton BEC systems — confirmed relationship |
| **Transfer function** | [REQUIRES PROTOTYPE MEASUREMENT] — power-to-length calibration curve must be established empirically |
| **Minimum blade length** | [REQUIRES PROTOTYPE MEASUREMENT] |
| **Maximum blade length** | Limited by waveguide length and power budget [REQUIRES PROTOTYPE MEASUREMENT] |

# **10. MINIMUM VIABLE PROOF-OF-CONCEPT EXPERIMENT**

The following experiment validates the core architecture at bench scale. Required before blade-length development proceeds.

| **ITEM** | **SPECIFICATION** |
| --- | --- |
| **Goal** | Demonstrate polariton condensate propagation through SWCNT waveguide at room temperature, initiated by EM coil, with measurable coherence at waveguide output |
| **Crystal** | CsPbBr3 single crystal perovskite microwire |
| **Waveguide** | SWCNT composite film on cylindrical substrate — 1 cm length |
| **Coil** | Custom solenoid wound to crystal phonon resonance frequency |
| **Drive source** | CW source at calibrated frequency |
| **Measurement — condensation** | Photoluminescence spectroscopy confirming nonlinear threshold behavior at crystal |
| **Measurement — propagation** | Interferometric coherence measurement at waveguide output |
| **Measurement — rigidity** | Mechanical probe contact force measurement under active vs. inactive condensate |
| **Success criteria** | (1) Condensation confirmed above threshold. (2) Coherence detected at waveguide output. (3) Measurable force differential between active and inactive states. |
| **Facility requirement** | University condensed matter optics laboratory — standard equipment |

# **11. OPEN ENGINEERING PROBLEMS — PRIORITY ORDER**

| **PRI** | **PROBLEM** | **DESCRIPTION** | **BLOCKING** |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | Condensate-waveguide rigidity | Structural rigidity under active condensate has not been demonstrated at any scale | Device viability |
| 2 | Blade waveguide scaling | No manufacturing pathway demonstrated for meter-scale SWCNT cylindrical lattice | Functional blade length |
| 3 | Crystal optical quality | Polariton lifetime requires crystal quality exceeding routine availability | Coherence length |
| 4 | Emitter nanofabrication | FIB milling of crystal emitter face to required geometry | Mode matching |
| 5 | Coil tuning protocol | Standardized procedure for crystal resonance measurement and matched coil winding | Repeatability |

# **12. PRIMARY REFERENCES**

| **REFERENCE** | **RELEVANCE** |
| --- | --- |
| Su et al. 2018 — Science Advances | Room temperature polariton condensate flow in CsPbBr3 microwire — 60 micrometer propagation |
| Wu et al. 2025 — Science Advances | CW polariton condensation at room temperature — 0.53 W/cm2 threshold |
| Kedziorowa et al. 2024 — Nature Materials | Predesigned perovskite crystal waveguides — template fabrication method |
| Graf et al. 2016 — Nature Communications | SWCNT polariton coupling — >110 meV Rabi splitting at room temperature |
| Held et al. 2024 — Nature Photonics | Electrical pumping of polaritons in SWCNT microcavities at room temperature |
| Ardizzone et al. 2022 — Nature | Polariton BEC in bound state in continuum — waveguide geometry |
| Ciuti et al. 1998 — Physical Review B | Polariton-polariton interaction constant — basis for blade interaction force |

**END OF SPECIFICATION  //  REV 1.0  //  RICKEY JAY BENNETT II  //  APRIL 2026**

AUTHOR: RICKEY JAY BENNETT II  //  APRIL 2026  //  CONFIDENTIAL RESEARCH DOCUMENT","stderr":""}

content.text:
Polariton condensates with long-range coherence propagate along the quantum wire at a high group velocity of 10 μm/ps, with some polaritons propagating over 60 μm at room temperature.

Novel technological applications significantly favor alternatives to electrons toward constructing low power–consuming, high-speed all-optical integrated optoelectronic devices. Polariton condensates, exhibiting high-speed coherent propagation and spin-based behavior, attract considerable interest for implementing the basic elements of integrated optoelectronic devices: switching, transport, and logic. However, the implementation of this coherent polariton condensate flow is typically limited to cryogenic temperatures, constrained by small exciton binding energy in most semiconductor microcavities. 

Here, we demonstrate the capability of long-range nonresonantly excited polariton condensate flow at room temperature in a one-dimensional all-inorganic cesium lead bromide (CsPbBr3) perovskite microwire microcavity. The polariton condensate exhibits high-speed propagation over macroscopic distances of 60 μm while still preserving the long-range off-diagonal order.

In this context, we demonstrate, to our best knowledge, the first experimental realization of coherent polariton condensate flow at room temperature in a 1D all-inorganic CsPbBr3 perovskite quantum wire microcavity by a nonresonant excitation. Polariton condensates with long-range coherence propagate along the quantum wire at a high group velocity of 10 μm/ps, with some polaritons propagating over 60 μm at room temperature. Moreover, we highlight that the actual polariton lifetime of 3 ps in our perovskite microcavity could be deduced through the interference fringes during the propagation process.

Polaritonic devices exploit the coherent coupling between excitonic and photonic degrees of freedom to perform highly nonlinear operations with low input powers. Most of the current results exploit excitons in epitaxially grown quantum wells and require low-temperature operation, while viable alternatives have yet to be found at room temperature. We show that large single-crystal flakes of two-dimensional layered perovskite are able to sustain strong polariton nonlinearities at room temperature without the need to be embedded in an optical cavity formed by highly reflecting mirrors. 

Strong light-matter coupling has already been observed in MAPbBr3 microwire/nanowire cavities (15); in particular, evidence for exciton-polariton condensation has recently been reported in all-inorganic perovskite CsPbX3 nanoplatelets (16, 17) and in spin-coated layered hybrid organic-inorganic perovskite thin films (18–20). Su et al. (21) have also shown polariton propagation in a CsPbBr3 microcavity wire over a distance of 60 μm. These results indicate huge room for substantial advancements in realization of low-threshold coherent light sources and polaritonic devices with this kin

However, to bring strong nonlinearities and good optical properties to room temperature (RT) is a real challenge. Recently, polariton condensation and superfluidity have been observed at RT in organic semiconductors due to the very large binding energy and oscillator strength of Frenkel excitons (5).

This investigation not only contributes to the advancement of our knowledge concerning the exceptional optical properties of perovskite-based polariton systems, but also unveils prospects for the exploration of WGM polariton condensation within the framework of a 3D perovskite-based platform, working at RT.

The unique characteristics of polariton condensate, including low excitation thresholds and ultrafast dynamics, open up unique opportunities for advancements in photonics and optoelectronics devices.

However, despite the promising initial reports and the attractive features of intrinsic WGM microcavities in perovskite crystals<sup>[23,33,34]</sup>, RT exciton polaritons and polariton condensation have not yet been demonstrated in this photonic platform.

In this framework, one-dimensional multimode WGM exciton-polariton condensation has

Here, we demonstrate the capability of long-range nonresonantly excited polariton condensate flow at room temperature in a one-dimensional all-inorganic cesium lead bromide (CsPbBr 3 ) perovskite microwire microcavity. The polariton condensate exhibits high-speed propagation over macroscopic distances of 60 μm while still preserving the long-range off-diagonal order.

In the past decade, a two-dimensional matter-light system called the microcavity exciton-polariton has emerged as a new promising candidate of Bose-Einstein condensation (BEC) in solids. Many pieces of important evidence of polariton BEC have been established recently in GaAs and CdTe microcavities at the liquid helium temperature, opening a door to rich many-body physics inaccessible in experiments before. Technological progress also made polariton BEC at room temperatures promising.

content.text:
Room-temperature steady-state polariton condensation enables CW perovskite lasers with ultralow thresholds.

Solution-processed semiconductor lasers are next-generation light sources for large-scale, bio-compatible and integrated photonics. However, overcoming their performance-cost trade-off to rival III-V laser functionalities is a long-standing challenge. Here, we demonstrate room-temperature continuous-wave perovskite polariton lasers exhibiting remarkably low thresholds of ~0.4 W cm−2, enabled by a variable single-crystal perovskite microcavity. The threshold outperforms state-of-the-art III-V lasers by ~30 times under optical pumping, and is exceptional among solution-processed lasers. The ultralow-threshold lasing arises from steady-state exciton-polariton condensation, a macroscopic quantum phenomenon akin to Bose-Einstein condensation.

content.text:
Despite the encouraging advances, the performance of perovskite lasers (or solution-processed lasers in general) is typically inferior to that of the best III-V semiconductor lasers, which show thresholds of down to ~12 W cm^−2^ under optical pumping ([27]). Further development in this direction is limited by the trade-off between quality and processing simplicity of solution-processed semiconductors.

Here, we demonstrate CW perovskite polariton lasers, achieving a remarkably low lasing threshold of ~0.4 W cm^−2^ at room temperature. The laser construction consists of a perovskite single crystal contained within a variable Fabry-Perot micro-resonator ([Fig F1]). The lasing thresholds are more than one order of magnitude lower than those achieved in state-of-the-art III-V semiconductor lasers under optical pumping ([27]–[29]), and are exceptional among solution-processed lasers.

Given their high charge carrier mobility and excellent photostability, SWCNTs represent a promising new avenue towards practical exciton-polariton devices operating at telecommunication wavelengths.

Exciton-polaritons are quasiparticles that have both light and matter character. 

Here, we report strong exciton-photon coupling in metal-clad microcavities filled with purified monochiral (6,5) SWCNTs and show that Rabi splitting above 110 meV can be achieved at room temperature. Exciton-polaritons were observed by angle-resolved reflectance and polariton emission measurements and were found to agree well with the coupled oscillator model and transfer-matrix simulations. We also investigate the influence of the SWCNT concentration within the cavity on the strength of light-matter coupling and on the polariton relaxation efficiency. Our experiments highlight the potential of SWCNTs for studying exciton-polariton phenomena in the NIR and pave the way to future applications of polaritons, for example, in the telecom domain.

content.title: Continuous transition between weak and ultrastrong coupling through exceptional points in carbon nanotube microcavity exciton–polaritons | Nature Photonics
content.text:
Non-perturbative coupling of photons and excitons produces hybrid particles, exciton–polaritons, which have exhibited a variety of many-body phenomena in various microcavity systems. However, the vacuum Rabi splitting (VRS), which defines the strength of photon–exciton coupling, is usually a single constant for a given system. Here, we have developed a unique architecture in which excitons in an aligned single-chirality carbon nanotube film interact with cavity photons in polarization-dependent manners. The system reveals ultrastrong coupling (VRS up to 329 meV or a coupling-strength-to-transition-energy ratio of 13.3%) for polarization parallel to the nanotube axis, whereas VRS is absent for perpendicular polarization. Between these two extremes, VRS is continuously tunable through polarization rotation with exceptional points separating crossing and anticrossing.



A microcavity exciton–polariton system based on aligned and packed single-walled carbon nanotubes exhibits ultrastrong coupling. The coupling strength is polarization sensitive. The record high value of vacuum Rabi splitting, 329 meV, is reported.

content.text:

We demonstrate the formation and tuning of charged trion-polaritons in polymer-sorted (6,5) single-walled carbon nanotubes in a planar metal-clad microcavity at room temperature. The positively charged trion-polaritons were induced by electrochemical doping and characterized by angle-resolved reflectance and photoluminescence spectroscopy. The doping level of the nanotubes within the microcavity was controlled by the applied bias and thus enabled tuning from mainly excitonic to a mixture of exciton and trion transitions. Mode splitting of more than 70 meV around the trion energy and emission from the new lower polariton branch corroborate a transition from exciton-polaritons (neutral) to trion-polaritons (charged). 

By exploiting the exceptional oscillator strength and sharp excitonic transition of (6,5) SWCNTs, we achieve large Rabi splitting (>110 meV), efficient polariton relaxation and narrow band emission (<15 meV).

We previously demonstrated neutral exciton-polaritons with a large Rabi splitting of more than 110 meV in simple metal-clad microcavities with (6,5) SWCNTs that could be excited optically and electrically and for which the coupling strength was tunable by field-effect induced charge accumulation. (9,45) Here, we report strong trion–photon coupling and observe emissive trion-polaritons at room temperature with an energy splitting of more than 70 meV. Reversible electrochemical doping of (6,5) SWCNTs in a metal-clad electrochromic cell enabled gradual tuning between neutral exciton-polaritons with ultrastrong coupling and charged trion-polaritons. The estimated charge-to-mass ratio was up to 200 times higher than that of electrons or holes in s-SWCNTs.

A team of physicists from CNR-Nanotec in Lecce, Università di Pavia, Princeton University and Université de Lyon has demonstrated Bose-Einstein condensation using a planar waveguide where semiconductor quantum wells were strongly coupled to a bound state in a continuum (BIC). In their paper published in the journal Nature, the group describes how they designed and built a BIC supported waveguide and used it to demonstrate polariton Bose-Einstein condensation.

In spite of several reports of optical BICs in patterned dielectric slabs with evidence of lasing, their potential as topologically protected states with theoretically infinite lifetime has not been fully exploited, yet. Here we show Bose-Einstein condensation of polaritons, hybrid light-matter excitations, occuring in a BIC thanks to its peculiar non-radiative nature.

Ardizzone and 14 other authors View PDF · Abstract:Optical bound states in the continuum (BIC) are peculiar topological states that, when realized in a planar photonic crystal lattice, are symmetry-protected from radiating in the far field despite lying within the light cone, i.e., in the energy-momentum dispersion region for which radiation can propagate out of the lattice plane. These BICs possess an invariant topological charge given by the winding number of the polarization vectors, similarly to vortices in quantum fluids, such as superfluid helium and atomic Bose-Einstein condensates.

Here we show Bose-Einstein condensation of polaritons, hybrid light-matter excitations, occuring in a BIC thanks to its peculiar non-radiative nature. 

The combination of the ultra-long BIC lifetime and the tight confinement of the waveguide geometry allow to achieve an extremely low threshold density for condensation, which is not reached in the dispersion minimum but at a saddle point in reciprocal space. content.title: Polariton condensation emerges from a bound state in the continuum – Physics World
content.text:
(Courtesy: Daniele Sanvitto/CNR-Nanotec Lecce) A bound state in the continuum (BIC) is a symmetry-protected topological state that, despite lying in the continuum radiation spectrum of a system, is unable to radiate in the far field.

Hard at work: Dario Ballarini (left), Vincenzo Ardizzone (centre), and Daniele Sanvitto in their lab. (Courtesy: Daniele Sanvitto/CNR-Nanotec Lecce) A bound state in the continuum (BIC) is a symmetry-protected topological state that, despite lying in the continuum radiation spectrum of a system, is unable to radiate in the far field. When supported by a photonic crystal, it is characterized by a supposedly infinite lifetime and a remarkable ability to enhance non-linear effects. Now, researchers in Italy, the US and France have utilized these properties to demonstrate polariton Bose-Einstein condensation in a planar waveguide in which semiconductor quantum wells are strongly coupled to a BIC. 

The particularly low excitation threshold of the system shows promise for creating easily-integrable hybrid light-matter optical circuits and quantum information processing systems.

Extremely high particle densities are required to create such condensates, so they are generally realized in high-quality optical microcavities with long photon confinement times. However, these microcavities require complicated fabrication processes and cannot be easily integrated into electronic devices. As an alternative to microcavities, planar waveguides have recently been shown to support increased polariton confinement and easy tuning of polariton-polariton interactions, as well as simpler integration. In this study, Vincenzo Ardizzone, a post-doctoral researcher at CNR-Nanotec in Lecce, and colleagues designed and built a planar waveguide that supported a BIC with zero intrinsic linewidth (i.e. an infinite lifetime).

content.title: Polaritons are Not Weakly Interacting: Direct Measurement of the   Polariton-Polariton Interaction Strength
content.text:
These interactions renormalize the polariton dispersion, leading to a continuous blue shift to higher emission energies as the polariton density increases. To lowest order, one can view the blue shift of the polariton emission line as the real self-energy due to the interactions, and the spectral width of the polariton emission line as the imaginary self-energy arising from the same interactions. When the particles undergo Bose-Einstein condensation, the spectral line width narrows due to the spontaneously emerged coherence.

Most previous theoretical work has assumed the exciton-exciton interaction strength calculated by Tassone and Yamamoto [20], found to be  $g \sim 6E_B a_B^2$ , where  $E_B$  is the excitonic binding energy, and  $a_B$  is the excitonic Bohr radius. Using the typical values for excitons in GaAs narrow quantum wells, namely  $E_B \sim 10$  meV and  $a_B \sim 100$  Å, gives  $g \sim 6$   $\mu \text{eV} \cdot \mu \text{m}^2$ . 

This, in turn, implies that the polariton gas is intrinsically weakly interacting, as measured by the unitless parameter  $\gamma = g/(\hbar^2/2m) \sim 0.01$  [21, 22], using the effective mass of polaritons  $m \sim 10^{-4} m_0$ , where  $m_0$  is the vacuum electron mass.

Under the mean-field approximation, at low particle density, the blue shift of ground state energy is linearly dependent on the particle density n, i.e.,

$$\Delta E = gn \tag{1}$$

where  $\Delta E$  and n are the blue shift and particle density, respectively. In the absence of many-body correlations, the slope g is density independent. In the experiments reported here, we measured the energy shift  $\Delta E$  of the polariton ground state, which has in-plane momentum  $k_{||} = 0$ , for various excitation densities. The interaction strength was then extracted as the slope of the energy shift with density.

content.title: Microscopic calculation of polariton scattering in semiconductor   microcavities
content.text:
Here, we use a recently developed microscopic description of polaritons involving electrons, holes, and photons, where the interactions between charged particles are assumed to be highly screened. Within this model, we perform an exact four-body calculation of the spin-polarized polariton-polariton and polariton-exciton interaction constants. In the limit of weak light-matter coupling relevant to an atomically thin semiconductor in a microcavity, we obtain excellent agreement with a recently proposed universal form of low-energy polariton-polariton scattering [O. Bleu et al., Phys. Rev. Res. 2, 043185 (2020)]. At stronger light-matter coupling, of relevance to multilayer microcavities, we observe that the interaction constant increases towards that predicted by the Born approximation. 

In particular, the nonlinear dynamics of a polariton condensate has been successfully modelled by an opendissipative Gross-Pitaevskii equation [12] with nonlinear interaction coefficients given by the polariton-polariton and polariton-exciton interaction constants  $g_{PP}$  and  $g_{PX}$ , respectively. Both of these are therefore of vital importance for an accurate modelling of polaritonic systems. While experimental measurements have historically differed from each other by several orders of magnitude [13, 14], recently there have been several high-precision measurements which have narrowed down the possible range of interaction constants [13, 15–18].

     9	## Overview

    11	This guide covers essential PDF processing operations using Python libraries and command-line tools. For advanced features, JavaScript libraries, and detailed examples, see REFERENCE.md. If you need to fill out a PDF form, read FORMS.md and follow its instructions.

    13	## Quick Start
    14	
    15	```python
    16	from pypdf import PdfReader, PdfWriter

    27	
    28	## Python Libraries
    29	
    30	### pypdf - Basic Operations
    31	
    32	#### Merge PDFs
    33	```python
    34	from pypdf import PdfWriter, PdfReader
    35	
    36	writer = PdfWriter()
    37	for pdf_file in ["doc1.pdf", "doc2.pdf", "doc3.pdf"]:
    38	    reader = PdfReader(pdf_file)

    42	with open("merged.pdf", "wb") as output:
    43	    writer.write(output)
    44	```
    45	
    46	#### Split PDF
    47	```python
    48	reader = PdfReader("input.pdf")
    49	for i, page in enumerate(reader.pages):
    50	    writer = PdfWriter()
    51	    writer.add_page(page)
    52	    with open(f"page_{i+1}.pdf", "wb") as output:
    53	        writer.write(output)
    54	```
    55	
    56	#### Extract Metadata
    57	```python
    58	reader = PdfReader("document.pdf")
    59	meta = reader.metadata
    60	print(f"Title: {meta.title}")
    61	print(f"Author: {meta.author}")

    63	print(f"Creator: {meta.creator}")
    64	```
    65	
    66	#### Rotate Pages
    67	```python
    68	reader = PdfReader("input.pdf")
    69	writer = PdfWriter()
    70	
    71	page = reader.pages[0]
    72	page.rotate(90)  # Rotate 90 degrees clockwise
    73	writer.add_page(page)

    75	with open("rotated.pdf", "wb") as output:
    76	    writer.write(output)

    78	
    79	### pdfplumber - Text and Table Extraction
    80	
    81	#### Extract Text with Layout
    82	```python
    83	import pdfplumber
    84	
    85	with pdfplumber.open("document.pdf") as pdf:
    86	    for page in pdf.pages:
    87	        text = page.extract_text()
    88	        print(text)
    89	```
    90	
    91	#### Extract Tables
    92	```python
    93	with pdfplumber.open("document.pdf") as pdf:
    94	    for i, page in enumerate(pdf.pages):
    95	        tables = page.extract_tables()
    96	        for j, table in enumerate(tables):
    97	            print(f"Table {j+1} on page {i+1}:")
